reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A lacunar syndrome characterised by prominent dysarthria together with clumsiness of one hand
The classic lesion lies in the basis pontis, though the internal capsule and corona radiata are also described
Facial weakness, tongue deviation, and a brisk reflex or extensor plantar may accompany the speech and hand signs
The clumsiness reflects mild pyramidal and coordination disturbance rather than dense weakness
There is no sensory loss, hemianopia, or cortical dysfunction, consistent with a lacunar mechanism
It is sometimes regarded as a variant within the spectrum of ataxic hemiparesis
Small-vessel disease from chronic hypertension and diabetes is the usual underlying cause
reference.pathophysiology: Dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome is a lacunar syndrome caused by a small deep infarct, typically from small-vessel occlusion related to hypertension and diabetes. The lesion, most often in the basis pontis or the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule, interrupts corticobulbar fibres supplying the bulbar musculature, producing dysarthria and often mild facial and tongue weakness, together with corticospinal fibres to the hand, producing clumsiness and impaired fine motor control. Because the lesion is small and spares sensory, visual, and cortical pathways, the deficit is limited to speech and hand dexterity with only mild associated pyramidal signs.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebellar lesion causing dysarthria and limb incoordination
Cortical infarct affecting the face and hand area
Demyelinating lesion of the pons or internal capsule
Bulbar presentation of a neuromuscular or motor neurone disorder
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI to detect a small pontine or capsular infarct
Assessment of vascular risk factors including blood pressure, glucose, and lipids
MR or CT angiography and carotid imaging to exclude large-vessel disease
ECG and cardiac evaluation to screen for an embolic source
Speech and swallowing assessment where dysarthria is marked
Repeat imaging where the initial scan is normal but signs persist
redFlags: Progressive or fluctuating deficit suggesting an evolving infarct
Any cortical sign indicating a non-lacunar mechanism
Marked dysphagia raising aspiration risk and suggesting wider bulbar involvement
Reduced consciousness or headache raising the possibility of haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: The syndrome usually carries a favourable prognosis with good recovery of speech and hand function after a single lacune, although recurrent small-vessel disease may lead to cumulative disability.
pitfalls: Dismissing isolated dysarthria and hand clumsiness as non-neurological or functional
Assuming a lacunar cause without excluding large-vessel or cardioembolic sources
Overlooking subtle cortical signs that would reclassify the syndrome
Relying on early CT, which often fails to reveal a small acute lacune
